utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Nice to be back after a fortnight's break. I hope you are a little more refreshed. Can we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleague Mr. Turone and Ms. van Dusschoten and Mr. Karin Khan. Mr. Khan is joining the Prosecution team, your Honours, because unfortunately Ms. Van Dusschoten is going to leave the Tribunal and will no longer be with us after the September sittings, so Mr. Khan will then take over in her place, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Congratulations, Mr. Khan. Nice to meet you. Can we have the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am Edina Residovic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic. With me is my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, attorney from Croatia, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic. With me is colleague Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo and defending Mr. Hazim Delic. With me in the team is Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning your Honours, I am John Ackerman and along with my co-counsel Cynthia McMurray -- something is wrong with the system here -- we represent Mr. Esad Landzo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we know what the Prosecution is about this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, your Honours, the Prosecution is ready to call Mr. Panzer, the witness, but before I do that, might I pick up from where we left off on the last occasion, if your Honours please, with respect to the outstanding motions. It is the Prosecution's intention, subject to the orders of the court, to call Witness R during the course of next week. There are two outstanding motions in relation to Witness R, one relating to the question of calling him in the first place and, secondly, the restrictive measures that we seek to have applied to him. At some convenient time to the court during the course of this week, if it is suitable to your Honours, we submit that it may be an appropriate time to hear those motions so that we can be in a position to call him next week, if it is convenient to the court. In the event that your Honours are prepared to hear us on those matters, Mr. Turone will argue the two motions that are outstanding in relation to Witness R. In relation to Witness S, we will be seeking to withdraw in relation to that witness, but I will leave that to Mr. Turone to formally do when he opens submissions in relation to Witness R.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is the Defence aware of these arguments which you want to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours, we filed motions -- your Honour, I may have mis-spoke. We are withdrawing in relation to Witness S, and proceeding in relation to Witness R, just in case I mis-spoke there. Yes, your Honours, we filed motions in relation to this on 22nd July 1997, so the motions have been filed for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I thought you were giving us Witness R.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are proceeding with witness R.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have decided to produce him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, we are proceeding with Witness R.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I know there was some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There was, your Honour. I hope that I have resolved the confusion now. We have advised the Defence that the list that they request is available. So Witness R we are proceeding with next week, Witness S we will seek to withdraw. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know whether the Defence is keen on arguing that this afternoon. If the Defence is interested in the argument this afternoon, at about 2.30, I will take that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the Defence of Mr. Delalic is concerned, we feel that we are ready to argue these motions today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: We agree that these motions be discussed this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if 2.30 pleases the court it pleases us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will take the argument on protective measures at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might? Just before the next witness is called, if I may address you briefly on a request that we filed on 29th August, requesting clarification on your order of 1st August 1997. Part of the contents of this request for clarification appear to have been resolved since we filed this request on 29th August because the Prosecution has indicated they intend to call officer Panzer in relation to the allegedly seized items from Vienna. There is a second part which is outstanding on which we sought clarification and that is the use of the word "verify" which is in your Honour's order, but is also used in the motion filed by the Prosecution on 1st August 1997. The Prosecution claims they can verify the proper procedures and chain of custody by calling these police officers. We hope there is no presumption in the use of the word "verification" and the issue is still outstanding and must be proven beyond all reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Definitely in every criminal Prosecution it remains until everything has been admitted and not before that. Verification does not necessarily mean a concluded admission of whatever has been tendered. It does not mean that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before perhaps one forgets, let me give a few announcements: according to our schedule, we are not sitting on Friday the 5th, we will be not be sitting. We also will not be sitting on Monday the 8th, these two dates, because we are taken over by another Trial Chamber. That is all for the time being. Can we have the Prosecution witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours pleases, I call Mr. Panzer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Lest I forget, there is another announcement I intend to make re the Prosecution motion on handwriting samples which is still outstanding for argument. We would like to take it on Wednesday morning at 10.00 am, 3rd September. That is before we start any other proceedings. Thank you very much. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly swear the witness? The interpreter should be sworn first. Swear the interpreter and the witness. THE INTERPRETER (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You can swear the witness. WOLFGANG PANZER (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Niemann. Examined by MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases. Sir, would you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Wolfgang Panzer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 12th May 1956.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a citizen of Austria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am an Austrian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a detective at the Vienna police department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what functions you perform in the Austrian police department and what unit you are attached to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I work for Division 1 of the Vienna police department. I work with several fellow officers in connection with the former Yugoslavia and the successor states.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position did you hold in March 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: District Inspector is what I am now and at the time I was team leader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you become a team leader prior to March 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since May 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the -- briefly describe to the Chamber the responsibilities and duties of a team leader as you performed them in 1996, March 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am in charge of all the case files that have to be processed and passed on to the court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many members did you have in your team in 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were four of us, so I worked together with three other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you name those three other people, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bycek, Moerbaur, Hiermann were the fellow officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1996, what was the nature of the crimes or the type of crimes that you investigated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Various areas were involved. Our division does not deal with criminal matters per se, our division deals with things related to national security and the protection of the state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In March 1996, can you tell the court when you first learnt of the circumstances relating to this matter in which you are now testifying in connection with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a Monday, 11th March, after the consultations. I was provided with a file that came from department 210, Interpol, and therein it was stated that one, Zdravko Mucic, who resided in the 17th District, should be investigated on a count of a request from the Federal Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told what role you were to perform in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To process the file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did that entail so far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gathered the information I could about Zdravko Mucic on the basis of the information in police records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you to be assisted in this process by any parties either inside or outside of your department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Monday I worked alone gathering this information. Other officers were not around for whatever reason, so I carried out this investigation on my own. Then it was Mr. Moerbaur, Mr. Bycek and myself who proceeded to gather further information about him, and the fourth person in the team, Mr. Hiermann, had been assigned to a different unit, he was working together with people from the Ministry of the Interior on a different case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any persons from the court assigned to assist with preparation of documentation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well Monday, on 11th March, I did not know at all that there was any connection with the International Tribunal. That only emerged in the course of discussion with the colleague from Interpol on 12th March, around noon time, then I learned that there was this request from the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you examine or read any documentation from the International Tribunal at that stage, or were you just simply informed of the interest of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Tuesday 12th, around 12.00, there was a meeting in our office and there were people from Interpol present. Mr. Gschwendt a supervising officer was there, a legal expert, Hiermann and our team, Mr. Moerbaur, Mr. Bycek and myself, and on that occasion I received a translation of the request for extradition from Belgrade that had been submitted to the Austrian Federal Ministry of Justice, and in that connection I was told in the course of the morning, that is to say on Tuesday 12th March at 10.00, there had been a discussion at the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say my superior authority, and the file I dealt with on Monday and that I passed on Tuesday, that that had been submitted to a representative of the Tribunal, Ms. Manke, and on the basis of the information I provided, a photo that I provided, it was confirmed that that individual was indeed Zdravko Mucic and as against the Interpol document, the first and last name indicated were right; the birth date indicated there was 1956 and the place of birth was mistaken, erroneous as well, so my task was to determine -- I am talking about what I was doing on Monday 11th -- whether that individual as described in the Interpol document was the same person as found in our registry and police files.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was an interest both from Belgrade and from the International Tribunal in relation to Mr. Mucic and it was in relation to both these requests for extradition that you were carrying out your enquiries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am only familiar with the document from the Belgrade Ministry of Justice that was submitted to the Austrian Ministry of Justice, and in that document it says that should Austria not extradite Mucic to Belgrade that he should then be prosecuted in Austria, and there was also reference made to the possibility of him being extradited upon a request by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I was not specifically asking about documentation, merely the fact that you knew the two organisations were interested. Moving on, what was the next stage you took in relation to this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next step was to ascertain whether Mucic was in Vienna at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you go about establishing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is the address at which he is registered with the police as living, so we checked that on a sporadic basis, as it were, and on 13th or 14th, I believe it was the 14th, we began putting that address under observation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in the observation of the address that you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was involved in that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next? What was the next stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tuesday and Wednesday, after two days of observation we were not sure he was there, we came up with a pretext and rang at his door and we asked about -- after the door was opened we asked about someone. First his daughter appeared, and she went and got her father, and at that point in time it was clear to us that Mr. Mucic did reside at the address indicated in the 17th District of Vienna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you had confirmed that what was the next step that you took?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me see now. On Tuesday 12th, in the course of the discussion with Interpol, the people there, Magister Gross, indicated that there was an arrest warrant against Zejnil Delalic. We were familiar with him by name from previous cases. The information we received from Interpol indicated that there should be joint action on the part of ourselves and the German police. Mr. Delalic was to be arrested in Munich; Mr. Mucic was to be arrested in Vienna. The whole matter was to take place on Tuesday 19th March at 6.00 in the morning. That was the plan. At the time we did not know whether the German police knew where Delalic was, so our task was, in the coming days, to establish whether Mr. Mucic was still living in the 17th District and to make it possible then to subsequently arrest him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to this arrest that was to take place on 19th March, was any documentation being prepared or prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, fellow officer Bycek dealt with that. There is the deposit, deposit 150 in the police headquarters, and he started preparing a document and he put -- filled in the relevant form. He put in the date, the name of the person, the address involved, and then on that document it is also indicated on what basis this was going ahead, that is to say there was a reference to the court, the fact that there was this court issued search warrant, and then the date that had been issued, so this preparatory work was carried out by Officer Bycek. I think that had been done on Saturday or Sunday evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document prepared by Officer Bycek, does that have a particular name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is referred to as a Niederschrift, a record and this is filled out on the spot and the grounds for a search are indicated and the seized items are listed there, so that is referred to -- that is what I referred to as deposit 150, that is the Niederschrift and a copy of that is handed over to the person involved, to the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it partly -- is it correct to say that it is partly prepared at the department and sometimes filled out at the premises where the search is being executed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a leading question. I would ask my learned friend not to ask leading questions. A sentence that starts "is it correct that" --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not need to be instructed in leading questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I would be grateful if my learned friend could wait until I have finished and not interject like that. It would be very helpful if my friend could not ask leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Actually, your Honour -- never mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It was rather leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour, I will rephrase the question. The Niederschrift document, where is that prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a form that is printed by the relevant authorities on behalf of the police. We have this in the police headquarters, police station, I fill it out, somebody else, whoever fills it out and it goes into the file for the court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But where is it actually completed and filled out? Is it completed and filled out in one place or a number of places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a rule, it is filled out at the premises where the search takes place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that rule universally followed, or are there exceptions to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The preparatory work, the fact that I fill some things in in advance, is just meant to make life easier for the officers who then complete the document at the premises. Let us take the case with -- it is an ongoing affair, there may be several searches that are involved in that case. I may, in fact, fill it out at the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that the Niederschrift document was prepared in connection with a search warrant. Who prepares the search warrant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The search warrant was drawn up by Dr Seda, the investigating judge from the Vienna district court. He issued both the search warrant and the arrest warrant. These can be issued only by a judge of the competent court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it Dr Seda was such a judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr Seda is a judge at the Vienna district court, he is an investigating judge, examining magistrate if you will, and he was in charge of all the procedures involving foreign countries, so that is the area for which the court has competence, that is what he dealt with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where does Dr Seda get the information from that he relies upon in order to draw up the search warrant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the security authorities of which I am a member. In this case, Dr Seda obtained the information from fellow officers at Interpol, and he was informed of this well in advance, in fact, because with Felsenstein from the Ministry of Justice, he had already been contacted in relation with the request for extradition from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the next step that you took in these proceedings in relation to this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Thursday 14th , there were these teams there at the address in the 17th District, keeping the address under observation, either there or in the 14th District at the INDA-Bau company. The observation was carried out on Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday, Monday until the time of the arrest of Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving up to the time of the arrest, can you tell us what time you arrived on the scene on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The arrest of Mr. Mucic occurred on Monday, 18th March at 2.15 pm in the 17th District of Vienna in front of Natagasse 11 and at that point in time, together with a fellow officer, I was 100 metres away from that house, Natagasse 11, because ten minutes before that he came to his car that was parked there and then he went back into the building, Moerbaur and Bycek --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "he went back into the building", who is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic. So the arrest was at 2.15 pm. You asked me where I was at that point in time. I was in the area of Natagasse 11 at my observation post, together with fellow officer Borlak. Prior to 2.15 pm, I do not know, some 5 or 10 minutes before that, Mr. Mucic came out to his car, he put a bag in there or something and then he went back into the building. Mr. Moerbaur and Mr. Bycek were at the INDA-Bau company. In the meantime, it must have been 2.10, something like that, I got in touch with my superior, Mr. Gschwendt and I told him by phone -- or to be correct, Mr. Gschwendt informed me that the German officers were going ahead with the arrest of Delalic, do we know where Mucic is, and I said yes, he has gone inside the building and I take it he is still there. Two minutes later, the phone rings again, Gschwendt gives me a call and says "the German officers have arrested Mr. Delalic in Munich, where is Mr. Mucic?" I said I cannot tell you exactly, but I assume he is in the apartment. At that point in time, Mr. Mucic comes out and goes to his car, so I tell Mr. Gschwendt, "he is back, let us get going", so that is when we went ahead with the arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a day earlier than had originally been planned as the day of the arrest, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Tuesday, 12th March, for the first time, Magister Gross informed us that both individuals should be arrested; that is to say one in Germany by the Germans and one in Vienna by us, and that these arrests should take place on Tuesday morning, the 19th, at 6.00 am. Now this matter was broached again on Saturday, that would be Saturday 16th May, in connection with the observation activities. We found that Zejnil Delalic was in Vienna. He was driving a vehicle with German licence plates, Munich licence plates at that, and he was driving from Taubergasse 15 over to INDA-Bau in the 16th District. The message we received said we would only go ahead with the arrest if both individuals are there or if we know where both individuals are because what we wanted to do was have the German officers arrest Delalic in Munich and go ahead with a search there in his apartment or on his company premises. On Saturday 16th we spotted only Mr. Delalic, and at that point in time we did not know where Mr. Mucic was. We did not proceed with the arrest, it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Delalic put under observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was observed that day, in the morning he came out of the building at Taubergasse and went back in. In the afternoon he drove to INDA-Bau. He went into the company premises there, he took out some folders, put them in the trunk of the car, hopped in the car and towards 3.00 pm he took the west autobahn, the motorway towards Salzburg and we assumed he was going on towards Munich from there. At around 5.30 pm at the Moserberg border crossing he entered Germany. At the time we took up contact with Magister Gross again and he said once again that the arrest should occur on Tuesday 19th March at 6.00 am. On Monday the 18th at 10.00 there was a meeting between a gentleman of the Tribunal, this was at Interpol's premises. There were people from Interpol, people from the Tribunal, and my superior, Mr. Gschwendt was there, and once again it was decided that the arrest would take place at 6.00 am on Tuesday unless the Germans were to arrest Mr. Mucic -- no, let me correct that, Mr. Delalic, by 4.00 pm; again only if we in Austria know where Mr. Mucic is, but the Germans went ahead and forgot about us, as it were. Fortunately we happened to know where Mr. Mucic was, and that is then how things proceeded. Mr. Delalic was arrested in Munich and Mr. Mucic was arrested in Vienna by our officers on Monday the 18th at 2.15 pm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the premises of Mr. Mucic on that day, March 18th, did you have that documentation with you that you described earlier in your evidence, namely the search warrant and the Niederschrift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had several files along. We had the court issued search warrants, and the Niederschrift were in there, because there were six places that were to be searched on the basis of a court order. Now in my folder I had the court issued arrest warrant against Mr. Mucic, the court issued search warrant for his apartment, Taubergasse 15, door 10, and the 150 document, the so-called Niederschrift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown Exhibit 151, please? Perhaps I could just have a look at it for a moment? (Handed). Could you look at this document you are now being shown, please? Do you recognise that document, Mr. Panzer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it, of course. This is the Niederschrift, this is this 150 document which was prepared in advance by Mr. Bycek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it all filled out by Mr. Bycek, or has some of it been filled out by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really say. He prepared it in advance. With regard to the information, this was filled in at police headquarters, I assume it was Officer Bycek, but I could not swear to it, but at all events, this was filled out at police headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see your signature appearing on this document at any place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is above my name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see on the second page of the document there is a reference to a number of listed items there. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This means that these items were found in the apartment pursuant to the search warrant and they were seized.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The handwriting that appears on the front page of the document which appears to be where the officers' names are inserted, do you know whose handwriting that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Mr. Borlak's handwriting. He was along with me in the apartment of Mr. Mucic. That is his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see a signature on the second page under that part which is entitled "signatures concerned/representative". Do you see a signature there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do see a signature. Mr. Mucic signed this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you there when he affixed his signature to this document? Were you present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the officers, I cannot tell you which now, but after everything took place, at the police headquarters -- only Borlak, Bycek, Moerbaur and myself were at police headquarters, that is 331 I am referring to. There was someone in the room, but I cannot tell you that I did see him sign it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although you may not have actually watched him affix his signature, were you in the room or nearby at the time, so far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the room throughout, just about all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any observations from the Defence about tendering it? What number is it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be admitted as Exhibit 151 and the English translation 151A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown document 163, please? (Handed). Mr. Panzer, I would ask you to look at this document you are now being shown. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise this document. This is the court issued search warrant relating to Zdravko Mucic and others. There is the six addresses where searches were carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the document you said that you had in your possession when you went to the premises on that day, 18th March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had this along.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender the search warrant, your Honour. It is numbered 163, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, that can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. Your Honours, is that a convenient moment before I move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, you can carry on. We will break in 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Panzer, you said in your evidence that you saw Mr. Mucic come back out to his car again after he had gone in and you had the conversation with your superior. What happened then? What happened when he came out to his car for the second time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Monday 18th then, shortly before 2.15 pm, I already knew Mr. Delalic had been arrested in Munich, and in the meantime Moerbaur and Bycek were called over from INDA-Bau. It took them about two minutes to come along, it is about two minutes away, it is just round the corner, and at 2.15 pm, Mr. Mucic went back to the car through the Meisengasse, it was a white Suzuki, it was parked in front of the building at Natagasse 11. He had a key and unlocked the door to the car. At that point in time, Mr. Moerbaur, Mr. Bycek, they had already arrived, along with myself and Officer Borlak, and we drove up to the level of Natagasse 11. Bycek and Moerbaur leapt out and Mr. Borlak, and I was at the wheel, so I was the last one to alight from the vehicle, and then at 2.15 pm Mr. Mucic was arrested on the sidewalk in front of the building at Natagasse 11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mucic restrained in any way at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean by restrained, if you please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he prevented from leaving or prevented from moving in any way, and in which way, if that is so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of Austrian law, when you arrest someone there is no question of leaving. Mr. Mucic was arrested, he was held. He had handcuffs put on with his hands behind his back as per regulations, and Mr. Mucic had absolutely no possibility at that point in time to leave for anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone say anything to Mr. Mucic at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Moerbaur spoke to Mr. Mucic. He told him first of all that he was under arrest pursuant to a court issued arrest warrant, and as -- this is as he was putting on the handcuffs. At that point in time I was already out of the car and I stepped up several feet to Mr. Mucic. I showed Mr. Mucic the warrant issued by the Vienna district court. I asked him whether he was Mr. Mucic. He said yes. There upon I told him that he was under arrest pursuant to a court issued arrest warrant, that he had the right to remain silent, that he had the right to have -- to notify a member of his family, and that he was entitled to consult a lawyer. I asked him whether he understood that, I addressed him in German. He said yes. In the course of our talk, he also told me and told Mr. Moerbaur, "oh, it is you, you were at my apartment a few days ago".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did he address that to when he said that? Who was Mr. Mucic addressing when he said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To me. You have to picture this. This is all in a side street in a two square metre big area. There are five people, the person arrested, Bycek, Borlak, Moerbaur and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the next thing to occur after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked him whether he had understood all that. He said yes, and he was very calm. He was not worked up or surprised or anything at all really. After that I told him that we also had a court issued search warrant which we were now going to execute. Fine, there upon we boarded the car, drove round the block and then entered the building Taubergasse 15, door 10. First we locked up the car, and then we went up to the apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that you had had a conversation with Mr. Mucic when he said you were the one that had come to the door. In what language was Mr. Mucic -- what language was Mr. Mucic using at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each and every conversation I had with Mucic, there were in fact only two of them, one -- I forget, that was Wednesday, Thursday, when we checked out to see if he was in the apartment and then when I talked to him at the time of the arrest in front of Natagasse 11, both of those conversations were in German. Mr. Mucic, on Wednesday, Thursday, we were in front of the apartment, when we had come up on the pretext to see if he was there, he answered my question in excellent German. When I asked him whether he understood why he had been arrested, he answered yes, and that conversation was in German as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then went to the apartment, the address that was mentioned on the search warrant, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. We went to the apartment. This was about five minutes after the arrest. He unlocked the apartment door and we entered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he, again who are you referring to? When he unlocked the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He, Mr. Mucic, or rather we had the key to the apartment, he had had that in his pocket. He handed it over, we uncked the door. He had his hands handcuffed behind his back and then we entered the apartment, Mr. Borlak, Mr. Bycek, Mr. Moerbaur and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic accompany you into the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. In the street I told him that we were going to proceed with a search and he said, "sure, let us go over".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you entered the apartment, was there anybody else in the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really remember, all I know is that we unlocked the door and very shortly thereafter from a neighbouring apartment his daughter Sanda came over, that is how I remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the apartment, the physical layout of the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a small hallway, kitchen, bathroom and three rooms. That is how I remember it. You go in and then on the right up against the window there is a small table, that is where we sat down and then behind that I think there was Sanda's room. To the left of that was the living room and then there was a connecting door there to the room which I believe was Mr. Mucic's room. That is all I can recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who, apart from you and Mr. Mucic, went into this apartment at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic, myself and the three police officers entered the apartment, Mr. Bycek, Mr. Borlak and Mr. Moerbaur. Very shortly thereafter, Sanda came into the apartment. That is how I remember it. I think she had been over at a neighbour's. We sat down and I said "Sanda, look here, we have got an arrest warrant for your daddy, a court issued search warrant. I have already explained everything to your father, everything we have to do pursuant to the code of criminal procedure, so if you would be so good, you could translate this for your father into Yugoslavian". Sanda did so and Mr. Mucic was acquainted then with the two warrants, not only in German but also in his native language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you have it translated considering that you had already been speaking to him in German?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a practice that I always use when dealing with foreigners. It is a preventative measure, as it were. When I say foreigner, I mean any non-Austrian. That is to preclude the possibility that such a person might later say in court that he did not know why and on what basis the operation was carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then have a conversation with Mr. Mucic concerning what it was that you were interested in finding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I talked to Mr. Mucic and I told him we were looking for documents relative to war crimes in Bosnia, in particular there were to be videotapes of Celebici camp that he had made and he said he did not have anything of the sort, but there were videos with footage from the Celebici camp. I asked, "where are those video tapes?" There upon we entered the living room and there is a piece of furniture there up against the wall and he took out some tapes, a dozen or so. He put those on the table and then he picked out from that pile four video tapes, and in respect of those he said that there were reports about the war, footage of destruction and footage of, shall we say, entertainment activities at the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the camp", did you understand that to mean any particular camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By "camp" what I am referring to is the Celebici camp, that is the only camp I am familiar with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The conversation you had with Mr. Mucic about these videos, was that conducted in the German language or was it being translated for him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in German.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he selected the four videos, did he then hand them to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took out the four videos. He told me that there were images of war events, including footage of him and then he handed those over to me. I asked whether we could have a quick look at them and he said yes, and I think Sanda, that is to say his daughter, turned on the VCR. I put the videos in there, Sanda perhaps used the remote control and then on fast forward had a look at a bit of footage. I saw some footage there. There were some officers, soldiers there, including Mr. Mucic, in uniform, so I did this with the videos, just had a quick look at them and then we seized those video tapes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the video tapes were being played on the VCR, did Mr. Mucic say anything at that time or did he remain silent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really say. It did not take very long. You have to picture the scene in the apartment at the time; there were four searches going on, Mucic's apartment. Then I briefly went up to Delalic's apartment. There the officers asked me something, then in the meantime Mr. Bycek went down to Zejnil Delalic's, to the premises of the BiH Club, the premises of the MAS Company. I was up and about and when I found the time I put in a videotape and had a quick look at it. As to whether he said anything, quite frankly, I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you seized the videos. What precisely did you do with them when you took the four videos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took the videos, put them on the table that we sat at after we came in, alongside other seized items which Mr. Borlak or Mr. Moerbaur had brought to me. Now as you can see on the record, the notebooks, the passports, the papers and the telephone information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you actually seized these videos, did anyone raise any objection or say anything to you about the seizure of the videos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides the four videos that you have mentioned, were any other videos seized by you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Mr. Mucic's apartment all we seized were the four video tapes. Just to play it safe, I had a look at the other video tapes. He told me that they contained movies, Sanda and he said that, and I put those in, just had a quick look, and in fact there were but movies on there, so they were not relevant to the case and I left those other video tapes in the apartment. So in Mr. Mucic's apartment all that we seized were those four video tapes, the four video tapes that he had handed me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that these video tapes were referred to among the other items in the Niederschrift or record document which is now Exhibit 151; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the entry made into Exhibit 151, the Niederschrift, in relation to the items that are mentioned on the second page? When was that actually put on to the Niederschrift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume that it was immediately after we reached police headquarters and we began the inventory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you not fill it out at the premises, as opposed to police headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the person concerned, i.e. Mr. Mucic, was taken by us to police headquarters, and we were going to be interviewing him and that is why it was not necessary to fill out this Niederschrift on the premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Physically, where did you put the videos when you were in the premises of Mr. Mucic in order to take them back to the police headquarters? What did you carry them in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The four video tapes and the items listed there were placed together on the table, the one we had set near the entrance, all items were placed in several plastic bags and taken to police station headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it they were taken to the police car and then taken to police headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went into plastic bags, then together with Mr. Mucic, we drove to police headquarters. These seized items had been placed in the trunk. We drove to police headquarters; Mr. Moerbaur, Mr. Bycek went up to room 331 with Mr. Mucic, Mr. Borlak and myself also went up to 331. Mr. Borlak was carrying the items seized at Delalic's apartment and I was carrying the items seized at Mucic's apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you carry the items seized at Mr. Mucic's apartment to the police car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two fellow officers from our department carried out the search in the apartment of Mr. Mucic. Mr. Moerbaur went up to Delalic's apartment and I went up to Delalic's apartment and they would ask "is this relevant, should this be seized or not?" After the search in Delalic's apartment was over I happened to see a gym bag there, I took that along and I put all the items seized in the apartment of Mr. Delalic in that. That bag, I took that to the car as well, and it said -- I think Mr. Borlak carried the things upstairs at police headquarters with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question though is who carried the items seized in Mr. Mucic's apartment to the police car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at police headquarters, who took the items seized from Mr. Mucic's apartment upstairs into police headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to, I think you said room 331, what did you then do with the items that had been seized from Mr. Mucic's apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all in the hallway I got hold of a cardboard box that happened to be lying there. I took that cardboard box and I put all the items from Mr. Mucic's apartment into that box, I stuck a white card on it, a reference card, as it were, and I wrote on that "search Mucic apartment Taubergasse 15, door 10", and then I wrote down the reference number of the court warrant and then I put that in a cabinet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this cabinet -- perhaps you might describe the cabinet for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Office furniture, one going from the floor to the ceiling, 60 or 70 centimetres deep, one that can be locked up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it have shelves in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several shelves, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you put the items that had been seized from Mr. Mucic's apartment, which at this stage was in the cardboard box, did you put it with any other items or was it on its own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There had been three searches where items had been seized, Mr. Mucic's apartment, Mr. Delalic's apartment and on the premises of the INDA-Bau company, the search carried out by Mr. Navrat. When we reached that office with Mr. Mucic and the seized items -- there had been a separation from the outset, because there had been the plastic bag in Mucic's apartment; then there had been the gym bag in which the items from Mr. Delalic had been placed, so all the items were always kept separate. There was never any possibility of there being any mixup, so even though everything already was separate for security reasons, everything was placed in a cardboard box and then the reference was put on there. In the meantime, Mr. Navrat turned up with the things he had seized, the folders and a box with the video tapes and the same procedure was followed there; a box was used, things put in there. Then there was this index, reference cards put on there and then on its own shelf in the cabinet, so for each of those was on each shelf, Mucic, Delalic and INDA-Bau.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Mr. Navrat brought the material that had been seized from INDA-Bau, can you recall who was in the room at the time when he brought them in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was Mr. Mucic who had been arrested, Mr. Borlak, Mr. Moerbaur, Mr. Bycek, myself, and in the room next door there were two other officers who were writing something about the search at Mr. Delalic's and they were just on the other side of a connecting door there, in the next office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you mind if you leave the next question to the next part of the session?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There is a matter I would like to raise before you rise, please. On 5th August this year, during the evidence of Officer Navrat, I drew to your Honours' attention the fact that whilst Navrat was still in the process of giving evidence, he was seen to be engaged over the luncheon adjournment in conversation with one Sabine Manke. The fact that Sabine Manke was talking to Officer Navrat whilst he was giving evidence was objectionable for a number of reasons. She is an employee of the OTP, and prima facie it is a serious impropriety for an employee of the OTP to be talking to a witness whilst that witness is on oath and giving evidence. Secondly, she is someone who has been engaged in investigating this case, as part of her duties. Prima facie that also makes it a serious matter for her to be talking to witnesses giving evidence in relation to this case. Thirdly, some weeks earlier, I had adverted to her presence during the evidence of Officer Moerbaur in the public gallery. She immediately left the public gallery, and was therefore on notice that she should not have anything to do with witnesses whilst giving evidence. Fourthly, because she had had something to do with transferring documents to The Hague from Vienna, she was a potential witness. At that stage, your Honours, my learned friend Mr. Niemann promised to make enquiries. He has not thus far, a month later, reported back to your Honours. I seek for him to give a report on the incident of 5th August. I invite him to tell us what steps have been taken in relation to this matter, and in order to establish a proper control over OTP employees and witnesses coming into contact whilst witnesses are giving evidence. We need to know what steps in particular have been taken in relation to the conduct of Sabine Manke on 5th August, and I would respectfully submit we ought to know why it has taken him so long to report back to your Honours as he indicated he would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I raise it now because, of course, we have a witness giving evidence in relation to this very matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I am happy to respond to that. First of all, the question of OTP employees speaking to witnesses, being offensive as it may to Mr. Greaves, of course, is not universally offensive in all jurisdictions. It may be in his jurisdiction but it is not in others. There is no prohibition on the practice here, so I suggest what may be objectionable to in England is not necessarily objectionable here. I would ask and invite him to give some authority for the proposition which he expounds, particularly authority based in international law. With respect to the question of speaking to witnesses, I had spoken to Ms. Sabine Manke, and I had asked her the nature of her conversation. It is quite common for employees of the OTP to speak to witnesses when they arrive, it happens on a regular basis, but it is always on the understanding that evidence of one witness against another is not compared. We are not suggesting that Ms. Sabine Manke is a witness in these proceedings. If Mr. Greaves chooses to make her one in the course of the Defence case, then he must bear the consequences of the fact that she has not been so nominated by the Prosecution. Your Honours, it is well understood by officers of the Prosecution that they are not to in any way manufacture evidence or endeavour to make a farce out of these proceedings. The officers of the Prosecutor are professional people, they are not in any way personally or in any other direct way involved in these proceedings, from a political or other point of view. They try to do their job in a professional way. We are not here to win, but to see that justice is done. I assure your Honours that officers of the Prosecutor behave in a proper and professional manner. They are aware of the consequences of speaking to witnesses, as is Ms. Sabine Manke, and your Honours, as far as the Prosecution is concerned, we are satisfied that there has been no attempt to fabricate the evidence of any of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think what Mr. Greaves is referring to is not a question of whether anything amiss has happened, but he wants your report on your undertaking you made to make an investigation. That is his main complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have done that, your Honours and I am satisfied that there is no impropriety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think before now, that is why he raised it. If perhaps such a report had been made before now, perhaps he might have not raised the issue at all, it would not have been necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Possibly so, your Honour, except I apprehend that Mr. Greaves is proceeding on a basis of ethical standards which apply in his own country and not necessarily in all jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There is still some suspicion that something amiss might be happening. I think it is fair that the Prosecution should take that into consideration in determining how its own witnesses or officials or possible witnesses would be associating with witnesses already who are in the Tribunal and are likely to give evidence, because the suspicion is still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the officers of the Prosecutor, it is imperative that they have access to witnesses, otherwise we simply cannot do our work and indeed we all from time to time have access to witnesses, but in so doing, we are aware of our professional responsibilities. I am satisfied that Ms. Sabine Manke is aware of her professional responsibilities and behaved in an appropriate and proper manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: One thing I am not able to understand, do ethical standards differ from country to country, what is good and what is bad? I do not think you have really national standards for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that in the United States, I will no doubt be corrected if I am wrong, but the concern of counsel talking to witnesses is not a concern. In the United States, counsel regularly proof witnesses and do so right through the proceedings. In some states, I am informed that indeed, counsel will speak to witnesses whilst they are indeed under cross-examination, which is not something I am familiar with, but I know that in other jurisdictions such as in England, counsel does not speak to witnesses. There are differences right throughout the world in relation to this. I understand in Europe it is not common for prosecutors to speak to witnesses. In the jurisdiction I come from, it is the same as the United States. Your Honours, there is a great deal of difference. In my submission, when we are in this situation, it is essential, your Honours, that the primary concern, and that is the fabricating of evidence, be avoided, but it does not necessarily have to be resolved in the way it is resolved in some jurisdictions, such as by putting prohibition on counsel from speaking to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I thought fabrication of evidence was unethical everywhere. That was the word you were using.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the very point I am making, your Honours, that it is essential that people be aware that the fabrication of evidence is something which is entirely unacceptable and completely unethical no matter where it happens, but the way to prevent it is not necessarily done the same way in every jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, any contribution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think Mr. Niemann may be labouring under some kind of misapprehension that Ms. Manke is not a witness. Ms. Sabine Manke has testified for the Office of the Prosecutor. I know that Mr. Niemann is new to the case and he may not have known that fact and I am sure that he was not aware of that when he made his statement a little earlier. I would suggest that Rule 90(d), along with the order from the Tadic case, decision on Defence motion to prevent contamination of testimony, which the court has discussed at some great length, would be the authority for Mr. Greaves' assertion that witnesses, be they witnesses off the street or employees of the Office of the Prosecutor, should not be discussing this case with other witnesses in this case. The one exception, of course, being Rule 90(e), that if it is the lead investigator for the Prosecution and has been designated as the lead investigator, then that witness can sit in the courtroom and is not prevented from being called as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Greaves' observation is a very pertinent one and I think he did not do anything more than reminding the Prosecutor about this undertaking, and as I said, if it had been already made, and then given to the Tribunal, this would never have arisen. Despite the differences in ethical standards, I think there is still a general one which will enable the Tribunal to ensure that justice is seen to be done, because if people outside who understand the situation appreciate that a Prosecution witness is getting too familiar with an official of that nature who also has already given evidence, this might raise a few eyebrows. But as far as you giving the undertaking, we expect you to ensure that it does not continue. That makes life better for everyone. I think we will have to break now and come back at 12.15. (11.45 am) (A short break) (12.15 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before we continue, may I say that we will still stop at 1.00 instead of eating into the lunch break. You have to be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If it may please the court, I would like to draw your attention to one thing. Several months ago, when the breaks were only 20 minutes, our clients were unable to leave the courtroom and the court at the time decided to have a half hour break. After today's break, I wish to inform the court that my client practically does not have ten minutes of break because the way the defendants exit and reenter the courtroom is organised in such a way that practically we do not have time to talk to our clients, nor does the client have time to have a cup of coffee and rest and be prepared for the continuation of the trial. Therefore, I would like to ask the court to give instructions to the Registrar to request organisation of the break in such a way that would allow our clients to have a rest during the break and to give their full attention to the continuation of the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we will try and arrange that so that the Registry can make the necessary adjustment to their movements.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We will do so, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases. Mr. Panzer, the cabinet that you had referred to earlier in your evidence in which the various items were placed, who had access to that particular cabinet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people who had access to that cabinet were Mr. Bycek, Mr. Moerbaur and myself, no one else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the room in which you operated I think you described as room 331, who had access to that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our fourth colleague, who was not there most of the time. Otherwise, it was only Mr. Bycek, Mr. Moerbaur and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The cabinet in which you placed these items, at the time that you put them in there, did the cabinet contain anything else or was it empty at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Completely empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the documents and items had been placed, including the videos, had been placed in the cabinet, did you then late in the day or during the course of the next day proceed to do anything with the items that had been put into the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The items that had been seized from Mr. Mucic, Mr. Delalic and the INDA-Bau firm were stored, sealed and the items from the search were put in a specific compartment and then late in the afternoon, in the evening of the Monday, that is the 18th, those items that were seized from Mr. Mucic were put in the inventory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By putting in the inventory, what does that entail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What it means is that -- it is basically the same thing, you have the document 150, and these items have to be catalogued or put in the inventory so we can access them later through the analysis report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the items themselves, did you do anything to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently deal with these particular items that had been seized yourself, personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The labelling procedure was carried out, that is to say you have a letter and then a figure. I did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you do the labelling procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the early evening, I think, for Mr. Mucic and for the other seized items it was in the morning of the Tuesday, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that Tuesday 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, the 19th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you labelled the items from Mr. Mucic's apartment, did you use any -- what particular letters and numbers did you use to identify those particular items?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The system was that I took letter M for Mucic, and the video cassettes were given M1A through to D, and the other documents, those I listed with M5, 6, 7. I cannot remember how far it actually went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned earlier in your evidence that during the course of this day, that is the 18th, that Mr. Navrat had come into the office and brought in some materials that he had seized; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall what it was that Mr. Navrat had brought in as a result of his search?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Navrat brought to me twelve folders with various papers, newspaper cuttings were there, and there was also a box with video cassettes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the twelve folders, did you do anything with them in terms of identification of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took a quick look at them with Mr. Moerbaur, just flicked through them and then put everything into a box and put them in the cabinet we described earlier. The drawing up of the inventory of the twelve folders and the cassettes only took place, I think it was the next day, Tuesday 19th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you drew up the inventory in relation to these items, the twelve folders and the videos that had been seized by officer Navrat, did you proceed to use the same identification labels as you had used from the items seized from Mr. Mucic's apartment, or did you do with them something different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically it was the same system, but there were a lot of video cassettes that had been seized, and so what we did was take I for INDA-Bau, I A, B, C, D, as we had with Mucic. You only have 26 letters, and for INDA-Bau I started with I for INDA-Bau and then the 12 folders and then the video cassettes. It was probably 13 to 64, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had marked each of these items with a label and after you had entered them in the inventory, what happened to the documents, the materials that were contained in the locked cabinet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That stayed with us until the analysis of the seized items. There was a report subsequent to the analysis and the items and the analysis report were passed on to the appropriate authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the appropriate authorities, are you able to tell us who they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way it works is that all the items that our department had went to the chancery of our division or department, it is then recorded and the seized items, plus this document, are taken by somebody from the police department in a vehicle to the place where they are stored in the district court. They are taken in there, that process is certified by a stamp, then these are sent to the competent judge, who was Dr Seda in this instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The analysis of the documents that you referred to that was carried out by the police, did you participate in that analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To a certain extent. All the documents were analysed by Mr. Moerbaur, Mr. Bycek and I gave some support with the video cassettes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you gave some support with the video cassettes, are you able to tell us what it was that you did with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The four seized cassettes from Mr. Mucic -- we looked at those and there were also the 26 from INDA-Bau and the 10 or 15 from Delalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown Exhibit 166? (Handed). Mr. Panzer, I would ask you to open this and go through the contents of that box and then I will ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I take them out?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do. Please take them out and look at them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Looking at the first ones here, these are the folders that -- I remember from what it says on the front of them there. I recognise them from what we have on the cover, I have my label, that is my signature that I put on there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, the witness pointed to the top right-hand corner of the exhibit. When you say the label, just give us the number of the label -- withdraw that. That label you then pointed to, is there any writing on that label?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this one you have I, then a dash and 1. In other words, it was the first folder that Mr. Navrat gave to me and that I listed or labelled with I for INDA-Bau, that is the first INDA-Bau folder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The I stands for INDA-Bau?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I stands for INDA-Bau.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the 1 stands for the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you go through each one of them now in order and see if you can see those labels and tell us if you see the labels, what is written on them? Just put them to one side, please, when you have done that for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one, I for INDA-Bau 1. I made that label myself. This one, I for INDA-Bau 2 is the figure. I did that. Here you can see I for INDA-Bau 4. I did that too. I for INDA-Bau 5, I did that too. I for INDA-Bau 9. That was me too. As far as I remember there were nine folders that were quite full of documents just for Mr. Mucic. There were all sorts of things, pay slips and that sort of thing. I for INDA-Bau 12, that was me. I for INDA-Bau 6, that was me, too. I for INDA-Bau 7, that was me, I put that on there. I for INDA-Bau 8. I wrote that. It is the document concerning the premises of Faukerplatz in the 5th District, it concerns a steak house Mr. Delalic and his brother were involved in. I for INDA-Bau 11, I wrote that and stuck the label on. I for INDA-Bau 10, I wrote and stuck that. I for INDA-Bau 3, I wrote and stuck that one, too. I am not sure about that. That probably has come off, I think. It should go with that cover, but there is my writing, I put that on too. As far as I remember, in this folder number 8, Mr. Moerbaur found the sentence by a Bosnian court, it was Mr. Mucic who was condemned in absentia, I think, 15 years, but in the other folders there were just newspaper cuttings concerning Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of what either you or members of your team did with the documentation that was contained in these twelve folders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only thing done with these documents was done by Mr. Moerbaur. No one else was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender those, your Honour. I tender the twelve folders as one exhibit, 166.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We object, your Honour. The whole issue of admissibility is one that has not been determined yet by this Tribunal in hearing evidence on this matter. It is premature to attempt to tender this evidence. That is our submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In my submission, your Honour, the question of tendering them, it has reached the point in the evidence where they should be tendered in the ordinary course of proceedings. It is appropriate for me now to seek to tender them, having regard to the stage of the evidence reached by this witness. If my friend has any objection to that, he may raise the objection now and we will deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What are your objections to the admissibility at this stage? The witness has already indicated he gave them those marks, having received these documents from the person who brought them.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There are several points I would like to make on that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We have been hearing evidence now over the last three months at different times, starting with Gschwendt and Moerbaur back in early June. The Prosecution has been held to strict proof on two counts; first that proper procedures were followed and that the chain of custody can both be proven, and in our submission it must be proven beyond all reasonable doubt. To determine that issue, final argumentation, based on what is going to be close on 1,000 pages of transcript, five or six Austrian police officers and one OTP investigator, is necessary. We received a letter from the Prosecutor last week saying that we would have final argumentation, he would be prepared to have final argumentation at some point after the testimony of Officer Panzer. So we are somewhat surprised now that halfway through the testimony of this witness, he is tendering evidence before the Tribunal. It is understood there will be final argumentation, both on fact and law, and we submit that should take place after Officer Panzer has been cross-examined and after the Prosecution decides that they have called enough evidence, in their estimation, when they think they can prove beyond reasonable doubt that procedures and chain of custody have been proven. It is premature, your Honours. What is more, at this point there has been no proof of the documents, which of course would be, in our submission, part of our final submissions. We have to consider everything that went on in Vienna and the whole transfer of those documents, the care, the handling, the processing and the transfer to this Tribunal, so it is premature, in our submission, to deal with these issues until final argumentation so that your Honours can evaluate all the evidence you have heard and review all the documents that have been tendered in support of all these alleged searches and seizures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I accept that the Prosecution has any other thing to say about these particular documents, and I think these are the documents he wishes to tender now, not all the others. There are still other documents which are coming, because all he is now saying is that the twelve files which he is now tendering are files which were so identified by this witness when they were brought to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But your Honour, to admit these twelve files, we have the issue of the chain of custody between Navrat, Moerbaur and this -- in our submission, it is premature to admit these. We have not even dealt with the final argumentation on the chain of custody issue, let alone proper procedures followed in Vienna in March and April. Your Honour should hear all of that evidence summarised and argued by counsel for the Defence before arriving at a conclusion, and, in fact, the Prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that those aspects of the search and seizure are proven. They have not done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Beyond reasonable doubt is a different matter, but I think it is for him to put up his argument as to why he thinks they ought to be admitted now without indicating how it came to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. Firstly the question of beyond reasonable doubt that counsel keeps referring to, I do not know the basis of that. It would be of great assistance to everybody if he could point to some authority in support of that proposition. If all documents had to be proved beyond reasonable doubt in the course of the trial, then I think that the concept known as circumstantial evidence would never exist. I am not aware of it and I am not aware of the need to be proved beyond reasonable doubt. There is nothing in the statute that suggests it has to be done. Certainly if the Prosecution wishes at the end of the day to rely on a document as proof of an element of the offence then that is a different matter, but it is not one single document in our submission that we are purporting to do that with, and in any event, that would be something that would happen very much later in the proceedings when it came to either the prima facie case or at the end of the proceedings altogether. In my submission, your Honour, there is no support for the proposition that these have to be proved beyond reasonable doubt at all. The rules governing admissibility are very well and clearly set out in the statute, my friend knows that, and they are the rules by which we are bound. Your Honours, these particular documents, as I said earlier, and counsel knows full well what these documents are sought to be tendered for, is the very issue which he complains about, and that is the chain of custody. These documents, your Honours, go to show that the documents were in a particular state, we have heard from Navrat as to the state that he found them in. The next stage of the proceeding is when they came to the police station, then this witness proceeded to deal with them, and in my submission, that is evidence of the chain. We are not seeking to rely on the contents of these documents for any other purpose than that, and in my submission, they are properly admissible, they are properly admissible now.
